item.title: Buccaneers K Chase McLaughlin set to play Thursday after landing on injury report
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Buccaneers kicker Chase McLaughlin was added to the injury report on Tuesday, but the team won't be adding a different kicker to handle the role against the Cowboys on Thursday night.
item.content:encoded:
Buccaneers kicker Chase McLaughlin was added to the injury report on Tuesday, but the team won't be adding a different kicker to handle the role against the Cowboys on Thursday night.

Head coach Todd Bowles said on Wednesday that McLaughlin will play in Dallas. McLaughlin was added to the report as a non-participant due to right hip and groin injuries.

McLaughlin is 9-of-9 on field goals and 7-of-7 on extra points so far this season.

Bowles also said that rookie linebacker Rueben Bain is expected to return after missing two games with groin and shoulder injuries. Quarterback Baker Mayfield (thumb), safety Antoine Winfield (rib), cornerback Benjamin Morrison (quad), and linebacker SirVocea Dennis (ankle, foot) have all been ruled out.

item.title: Will Reichard named NFC special teams player of the week
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: The Vikings may not have reached the end zone in Sunday’s 15-10 victory over the Dolphins, but they did have an accurate kicker.
item.content:encoded:
The Vikings may not have reached the end zone in Sunday’s 15-10 victory over the Dolphins, but they did have an accurate kicker.

That’s why Will Reichard has been named NFC special teams player of the week.

Reichard hit on all five of his field goal attempts from 47, 50, 33, 41, and 29 yards to score all 15 of Minnesota’s points.

This is Reichard’s first career player of the week award. He’s the third Vikings player to earn the honor this season following Isaiah Rodgers in Week 2 and Myles Price in Week 3.

item.title: Chiefs P Matt Araiza named the AFC special teams player of the week
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Chiefs punter Matt Araiza used his feet to help the team in multiple ways in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Chiefs punter Matt Araiza used his feet to help the team in multiple ways in Week 4.

Araiza had five punts against the Raiders and all of them landed inside of the Las Vegas 20-yard-line with one pinning the Raiders inside the 5-yard-line. Araiza also converted a fake punt with a 12-yard run in the first quarter of the 30-27 win.

The NFL announced on Wednesday that Araiza has been named the AFC special teams player of the week. It's the first time that Araiza has earned that honor.

Araiza averaged 47.6 yards per punt last Sunday and is averaging 52.3 yards per kick for the entire season.

item.title: Jaguars LB Foye Oluokun is the AFC defensive player of the week
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Jaguars continued their impressive start to the season against the Bengals last Sunday and linebacker Foye Oluokun was integral to their success.
item.content:encoded:
The Jaguars continued their impressive start to the season against the Bengals last Sunday and linebacker Foye Oluokun was integral to their success.

Oluokun had seven tackles, an interception, a forced fumble and a quarterback hit to help the Jags to a 22-17 win. The interception came at Jacksonville's 10-yard-line early in the fourth quarter and kept the Jaguars up 16-10 heading into the final minutes of the contest.

On Wednesday, the NFL announced that Oluokun has been named the AFC defensive player of the week.

It is the fourth time Oluokun has been awarded conference player of the week honors. The first two came while he was with the Falcons and the last two have come since he moved on to the Jaguars.

item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Panthers receiver Tetairoa McMillan was dominant in Sunday's victory over the Lions and now the league has recognized him for his performance.
item.content:encoded:
Panthers receiver Tetairoa McMillan was dominant in Sunday's victory over the Lions and now the league has recognized him for his performance.

McMillan has been named NFC offensive player of the week.

McMillan caught 14 passes for 192 yards with two touchdowns in the 32-26 victory, setting career highs in both catches and yards.

McMillan is the first receiver in Panthers franchise history to win NFC offensive player of the week.

He tied the Panthers franchise record for receptions in a single game on Sunday.

McMillan will get a chance to rest after so many catches, as he and the Panthers have a Week 5 bye.

item.title: Drake Maye named the AFC offensive player of the week
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Patriots quarterback Drake Maye's first three games raised a lot of red flags around New England, but they are harder to find after last Sunday's win over the Bills.
item.content:encoded:
Patriots quarterback Drake Maye's first three games raised a lot of red flags around New England, but they are harder to find after last Sunday's win over the Bills.

Maye went 22-of-37 for 269 yards and three touchdowns, including one that wide receiver Efton Chism used one hand to secure for the winning points in a 29-26 victory. Maye also ran eight times for 54 yards.

The NFL announced on Wednesday that the performance landed Maye recognition as the AFC offensive player of the week. It is the second time that Maye has won the award.

Maye did have a pair of turnovers in the game after having seven in the first three games, so there's still some work to do to get back to his 2025 level of play. The overall effort provided reason to believe that can happen and that was the best development of the week for the Patriots.

item.title: Eagles to sign RB Dameon Pierce to 53-man roster
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Eagles are making a move to bolster their ailing running back group.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles are making a move to bolster their ailing running back group.

Jeremy Fowler of ESPN reports that they will sign Dameon Pierce to the active roster from the practice squad.

Pierce signed with the Eagles in March and returned to the practice squad after being released at the end of the summer. He had four carries for 10 yards in one game for the Chiefs and 10 carries for 26 yards in four games for the Texans last year. He also spent the previous three seasons with the Texans and had 415 carries for 1,674 yards and eight touchdowns over his entire run in Houston.

Saquon Barkley and Tank Bigsby both left last Sunday's loss to the Rams with injuries. Barkley hurt his hamstring and is questionable for the near future while Bigsby suffered a core muscle injury that requires surgery.

item.title: 1989 book claimed that "no fewer than 70" NFL games had been fixed
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The cesspool that is social media often kicks out some bubbling crude.
item.content:encoded:
The cesspool that is social media often kicks out some bubbling crude. (Oil, that is.)

A clip from a 1989 episode of The Pat Sajak Show (yes, Wheel of Fortune was once so popular that the host got a late-night show, for 15 months) has been making the rounds on Twitter. In it, Don Moldea discusses his book, Interference: How Organized Crime Influences Professional Football.

During the nearly eight-minute interview, Moldea makes some startling claims.

He says that "no fewer than 26" past and present team owners have documented ties to the gambling community and/or organized crime. Moldea also contends that, as of 1989, "no fewer than 70 NFL games have been fixed."

Moldea's claim was bolstered by bookmaker Don Dawson admitting to participating in the fixing of no fewer than 32 games. Dawson told Moldea that he rigged the final scores by working with the quarterback.

Moldea says that his book names players who were involved in fixing games, and that it identifies eight specific 1979 games that were fixed by two referees who were later investigated by the FBI and the IRS.

So how did none of this ever come to light at the time it was happening?

"No fewer than 50 legitimate investigations of corruption within the NFL have been either suppressed or just flat-out killed as a result of a sweetheart relationship between NFL Security, which is the internal police force within the league, and a variety of federal and state and local law-enforcement agencies," Moldea contends.

Sajak somewhat jokingly asks Moldea if he fears for his safety, given that the book delves into issues of organized crime.

"No one's tried to kill me in almost six years," Moldea says.

Thirty-seven years later, Moldea's book resonates. Especially with legalized gambling in most states and prediction market-style gambling in all states.

I've found and ordered a copy of the book. And Moldea apparently has yet to be whacked; we may have to track him down for more details.

item.title: Odell Beckham Jr. joins Vikings practice squad
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Beckham is reuniting with HC Kevin O'Connell, who was his OC with the Rams in 2021.
item.content:encoded:
Odell Beckham Jr. is headed for another reunion.

Beckham is signing with the Vikings practice squad, Minnesota announced on Wednesday.

Minnesota head coach Kevin O'Connell was the Rams' offensive coordinator when Beckham won Super Bowl LVI with Los Angeles to cap the 2021 season.

Beckham caught 27 passes for 305 yards with five touchdowns in eight regular-season games for the Rams that year. He then had 21 receptions for 288 yards with two TDs in the postseason before tearing his ACL in the Super Bowl.

While Beckham appeared in three games for the Giants this season, he did not catch a pass.

The Vikings have also signed receiver Jeshaun Jones to their practice squad.

Center Michael Jurgens and tight end Ben Yurosek have also returned to practice from injured reserve.

item.title: NFL rescinds Kyle Juszczyk's beer chugging celebration fine
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Juszczyk appealed the fine and said his celebration was tied to his "Juice" nickname.
item.content:encoded:
49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk was one of the players fined by the NFL for mimicking drinking a beer during celebrations earlier this season, but he won't have to pay it.

Adam Schefter of ESPN reports that Juszczyk's fine has been rescinded after an appeal. Juszczyk argued that he has done the celebration throughout his career without receiving any discipline for the act and that it references his nickname "Juice" rather than the alcoholic beverage.

It appears that point was central to the decision to overturn the fine as the league said they came to the decision “because his celebration was simulating drinking a juice box, not a beer." Schefter also notes that Juszczyk pointed out the "hypocritical" nature of the league fining a player for drinking a beer while also receiving sponsorships from beer companies.

Colts guard Matt Goncalves was fined for the same reason, but there's been no word of any change to his punishment.

item.title: Nick Sirianni: More answers Wednesday on Saquon Barkley's status
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Eagles running back Saquon Barkley's status for Week 5's game against the Jaguars in London is up in the air.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles running back Saquon Barkley's status for Week 5's game against the Jaguars in London is up in the air.

Barkley left Sunday's 24-20 loss to the Rams with a hamstring injury and head coach Nick Sirianni said the team will have a better idea later this week about whether Barkley is going to miss time.

"Yeah, we'll see. These guys are going through different things with treatment and all those different things," Sirianni said, via a transcript from the team. "We'll see how everything responds and then have more answers for you probably Wednesday on that stuff. I know he'll do everything he can do to get himself back, and obviously, he's a great player and a great teammate. We always need him on the field."

Barkley had two carries for eight yards on Sunday. He also missed most of Week 2 with a stinger and has 36 carries for 182 yards on the season.

Tank Bigsby is set for core muscle surgery after getting hurt against the Rams, so the Eagles are going to be shorthanded at running back even if Barkley is able to go this week. Will Shipley is the only healthy back on the 53-man roster.

item.title: NFL Referees Association objects to "severity" of suspensions of Adrian Hill, Jeff Seeman
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFLRA contends the punishments exceed past disciplinary practices.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL Referees Association believes the league is being over-officious when it comes to the discipline imposed on a pair of officials.

Referee Adrian Hill (pictured) was suspended one game for his interaction with Vikings linebacker Eric Wilson. Line judge Jeff Seeman was suspended two games for the comments he made to Cardinals tight end Trey McBride.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the union representing the NFL's game officials said this: "The NFL Referees Association believes the suspensions imposed by the NFL on two officials following incidents this past weekend were excessive and inconsistent with past precedent. Given these concerns, the NFLRA will challenge the severity of those suspensions and meet with the NFL Officiating Department to discuss the League's disciplinary standards. The association also plans to meet with NFL Players Association leadership to address on-field conduct and the growing levels of confrontation between players and officials."

The statement also included a quote from NFLRA executive director Scott Green.

“NFL officials have a responsibility to conduct themselves professionally on the field, and the actions in these incidents fell short of that standard," Green said. "Accountability matters, but that should not result in discipline that is excessive or inconsistent with established precedent.

“Officials are routinely subjected to highly charged interactions and, at times, verbal abuse from players and coaches. While that never excuses misconduct by an official, it shouldn't be dismissed as simply part of the game. The League expects the highest level of professionalism from its officials, and it should demand the same from everyone on the field.

“We will defend the principle that discipline must be fair, consistent and proportionate. Holding officials accountable while ignoring or minimizing the conduct directed at them is neither fair nor an effective way to address this issue. We look forward to working with the League and NFLPA toward that shared goal.”

Ultimately, it's a labor-management issue. The league has created a workplace precedent over the years when it comes to discipline. The NFLRA will argue that the punishment exceeds the established pattern and practice. And the arbitration procedures in the collective bargaining agreement between the NFL and the NFLRA will drive the final analysis.

item.description: The Steelers made an addition to their 53-man roster on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Steelers made an addition to their 53-man roster on Tuesday.

They announced that they have signed cornerback Terrell Smith off of the Commanders' practice squad. They had an open roster spot after making other moves on Monday, so there was no need to make a corresponding drop from the active roster.

Smith was a Bears fifth-round pick in 2023 and he played in 26 games over his first two seasons. He tore his patellar tendon last year and was signed by Washington after being cut in Chicago this summer.

Smith has 68 tackles, an interception, 10 passes defensed, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery while with the Bears.

The Steelers also announced that they have signed defensive lineman K.J. Henry to the practice squad. Linebacker Bradyn Swinson was released to open a spot for him.

item.title: Eagles DC Vic Fangio: Number of snaps impacted defense against Rams, but have to finish
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Eagles had a 20-10 lead over the Rams deep into the fourth quarter of last Sunday's game against the Rams, but they wound up losing when the Rams scored back-to-back touchdowns in the final four minutes of the game.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles had a 20-10 lead over the Rams deep into the fourth quarter of last Sunday's game against the Rams, but they wound up losing when the Rams scored back-to-back touchdowns in the final four minutes of the game.

The first Rams scoring drive started at their own 2-yard-line and the second covered 79 yards. Los Angeles only faced two third downs on the 21 snaps that made up those possessions, which led to a question for Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio about whether the cumulative effect of being on the field for 82 snaps — including penalties, but excluding one kneeldown at the end of the game — wore the unit down.

"Well, I'm not going to insult your or anybody's intelligence that yeah, it has an effect, but we got to find a way to finish," Fangio said, via a transcript from the team.

The Eagles couldn't finish on either side of the ball against the Rams. If the offense continues to fail to do so in the future, the job Fangio and the defense will have to do for the team to win games will only get more difficult.

item.title: Steelers-Browns racks up 16.59 million viewers on Prime Video
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: More than a few people saw Thursday night's F-bomb interaction between Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers and coach Mike McCarthy.
item.content:encoded:
More than a few people saw Thursday night's F-bomb interaction between Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers and coach Mike McCarthy.

The Week 4 Thursday night game on Prime Video averaged 16.59 million viewers.

It's a 19-percent increase over last year's Week 4 Thursday night meeting between the Seahawks and Cardinals. That game averaged 13.94 million viewers.

The number, per Amazon, made it the most-watched Week 4 Thursday night game since Prime Video assumed the package in 2022.

An unresolved question lingers as to whether Amazon is goosing the numbers by autoplaying the game for anyone who visits their Prime page while the game is being televised. The higher numbers are obviously good for Amazon, and in turn good for the NFL.

Either way, Thursday Night Football is here to stay. The only question is whether and when it will be joined by a Tuesday night and/or Wednesday night effort on a weekly basis.

item.title: Dan Campbell: We won't accept mediocrity on either side of the ball
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Saints knocked the Lions out of the top spot for points allowed on Monday night, but being anywhere near the top of that list is not where teams want to be four weeks into the season.
item.content:encoded:
The Saints knocked the Lions out of the top spot for points allowed on Monday night, but being anywhere near the top of that list is not where teams want to be four weeks into the season.

Detroit has allowed at least 24 points and 355 yards in each of their four games, which led to head coach Dan Campbell's vote of confidence for defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard after Sunday night's loss to the Panthers. During an appearance on 97.1 The Ticket on Tuesday, Campbell pointed to a lack of discipline and a lack of trust among players on the unit as reasons why the defense has been so easily torn apart. He added that others will get opportunities as the team looks for the right mix to improve their results.

"We’re going to give some other guys an opportunity, and go, man. But we’re not going to accept mediocrity. That’s not what we’re doing here," Campbell said. "We've got too many guys playing at a high level, and we’re going to raise the floor on this team."

The Lions offense ranks fifth in the league in points scored, but some have wondered if the defense's inability to get stops has an adverse effect on the offense. Campbell was asked about that, but said he thinks the team has been "average" across the board and that the offense has room to improve alongside the defense.

"Man, if you want to be great, they should want to score 35 points a game, at a minimum," Campbell said. "That’s what greatness is. That’s what they’re charged with. We've got plenty of weapons on offense and if we’re gonna accept mediocrity, then yeah, we can make all the excuses in the world. If we want to spit and sputter and be average, that’s one thing. We’re not going to be average. We’re going to raise the floor on these guys, man. We’re going to push ‘em. We've got too much offensively right now. Our quarterback’s too good, our playmakers are too good, and we've got a young, hungry offensive line that’s got a ton of room to grow."

Campbell was adamant this summer that the Lions' Super Bowl window is not closed, but the first four weeks haven't done much to support the feeling that big things are in store for the team this season. That will need to change quickly if they want to avoid calls for more sweeping changes to how business is getting done in Detroit.

item.title: North Carolina hires search firm to help find new G.M. to work with Bill Belichick
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: North Carolina's ongoing support, fulsome or not, of coach Bill Belichick comes with expectations.
item.content:encoded:
North Carolina's ongoing support, fulsome or not, of coach Bill Belichick comes with expectations. One of these expectations will be that he won't hire aa crony or a family member to be the next G.M. of the program.

In the aftermath of G.M. Mike Lombardi and defensive coordinator Steve Belichick resigning amid an investigation regarding various still-unspecified irregularities within the program, UNC is looking for a new General Manager. And the program isn't letting Belichick simply bring in someone with whom he is already comfortable.

Via Brian Murphy of WRAL, North Carolina has hired Sean Magee of Turnkey ZRG to assist with the search for Lombardi's replacement.

Magee previously was the G.M. at Michigan, and he has a degree from Navy. Which could make Belichick inclined to cooperate with Magee, given Belichick's affinity for the Naval Academy. (His dad was a longtime scout there, and it was a moth-eaten Navy sweatshirt that Belichick was wearing in the 2025 CBS softball interview that was treated by Belichick and his handler as chin music.)

“I am really looking forward to working with Sean, given his many years of high-level executive leadership experience in both professional and collegiate football,” Belichick said in a statement.

In light of Belichick's tenuous status in Chapel Hill, the job may not be a desirable one. Unless the program hires someone who regards it as an opportunity to help shape the direction of the program without Belichick in 2027.

Either way, the clock is ticking. Recruiting never ends, and the Tar Heels have gone more than two months without a G.M. on the job, due to Lombardi being placed on paid leave before he abruptly decided to walk away from the job.

Even if Belichick isn't fired, he could decide after the dust settles on the 2026 season that he, too, has had enough. The investigation, which at one point seemed to be looking for anything it could find to justify firing the head coach without pay, may have prompted Belichick to react to the probe that took out both his consigliere and his son by treating the current season as his last ride with the Tar Heels.

item.title: Eagles RT Lane Johnson announces retirement
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: He played 171 games in 14 seasons with the Eagles, who made him a first-round pick in 2013.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles right tackle Lane Johnson was unexpectedly scratched from the lineup on Sunday, with the team citing "personal reasons." On Tuesday, he announced his retirement.

"I have given it my all for 14 years, season after season pushing my body to the max and tirelessly working my craft to not only live up to the legacy of the guys that came before me, but to set a new standard of success for the best franchise in all of sports," Johnson wrote, in part, in a statement on social media. "I deeply wanted to gut it out for one more year, to take the field with my brothers for one last season. But after a lot of reflection, I've realized that my personal and family priorities in my life have changed. Right now, it is critical that I focus on my mental health. I owe it to my teammates, coaches, the organization and the fans to have my head and heart 100 percent in the game. And right now, my heart is telling me that it's time to say goodbye to football.

"At this time, I have made the incredibly difficult decision to retire from the National Football League."

Johnson missed time at the start of training camp and said his mother had been dealing with some health issues when he returned to the team.

The Eagles lost on Sunday, dropping their record to 18-30 without Johnson and 122-63-1 with him since drafting him in the first round in 2013.

Johnson, 36, is a six-time Pro Bowler and was first-team All-Pro twice. He started 171 career regular-season games and 15 in the postseason, and Johnson won two Super Bowl rings.

He missed seven games last season with a Lisfranc foot injury.

5. Seahawks (No. 6; 3-1): Let Rashid cook.

11. Raiders (No. 15; 3-1): Even though they lost, the Raiders must be regarded as a contender.

15. Bengals (No. 7; 2-2): The Super Bowl pipe dream is quickly imploding.

16. Giants (No. 16; 3-1): Giants fans will age like presidents with Jameis Winston playing quarterback.

19. Panthers (No. 26; 2-2): Bryce Young is getting better and better all the time.

20. Falcons (No. 22; 2-2): Just give the ball to a Robinson on every play.

21. Lions (No. 14; 2-2): The Super Bowl window sure seems closed.

22. Colts (No. 24; 2-2): Can they win enough games to steal a wild-card berth?

23. Packers (No. 25; 2-2): It never felt like they truly wanted to beat the Buccaneers.

24. Texans (No. 17; 0-4): Where did the Houston defense go?

25. Saints (No. 19; 1-3): They've improved, but not nearly enough to contend.

26. Commanders (No. 23; 1-3): It's getting late early for the Commanders and coach Dan Quinn.

27. Cardinals (No. 27; 1-3): With each Chargers' loss, the Week 1 win looks less impressive.

28. Jets (No. 28; 1-3): Woody Johnson may soon be tempted to let Mike Tomlin build Minecraft Manhattan.

29. Chargers (No. 29; 0-4): Andrew Luck retired and stopped playing. Justin Herbert has apparently retired and kept playing.

30. Buccaneers (No. 30; 0-4): It could get very ugly on Thursday night in Dallas.

31. Titans (No. 31; 0-4): They're getting a new stadium. One of these days, they'll get a new team.

32. Dolphins (No. 32; 0-4): Could the first team to go 17-0 go 0-17?

The Colts have added a veteran defensive end ahead of Week 5.

The team announced that they have signed Carl Lawson to their practice squad. Tight end Kenny Fletcher was released in a corresponding move.

Lawson played in one game for the Ravens last season and he's played in 90 games since the Bengals made him a fourth-round pick in 2017. He spent four seasons in Cincinnati and played for current Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo in his last two years with the team.

Lawson moved on to the Jets and spent three seasons with them — he missed all of the 2021 season with a torn Achilles — and played for the Cowboys in 2024. He has 135 tackles, 32 sacks, four forced fumbles and a fumble recovery over his entire career.

item.title: Bills DC Jim Leonhard: We have to make home crowd an advantage for us
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Home field advantage is something that is talked about often in the NFL, but Bills cornerback Dee Alford didn't feel much of one during last Sunday's loss to the Patriots.
item.content:encoded:
Home field advantage is something that is talked about often in the NFL, but Bills cornerback Dee Alford didn't feel much of one during last Sunday's loss to the Patriots.

Alford said, via Nick Suss of ESPN.com, that the crowd at Highmark Stadium can get "super loud to the point where we're not able to get the play as fast as we need it" and that leaves the defense scrambling because of communication breakdowns. During a press conference this week, Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard was asked about Alford's comments.

Leonhard acknowledged the difficulties that can arise in a loud environment, but said that the opposing team faces more of them and that the Bills have to view the home crowd into a plus rather than an obstacle.

"It's always harder to communicate at home than it is on the road. If we complain about that, we are a———s," Leonhard said. "We have to turn that into the biggest advantage we have. As hard as it is for us, it's significantly harder for an offense. We have to find a way to make that an advantage for us. If we ever use that as a cop out — I have to be smart in how we game plan. There’s certain things you can do on the road that are a little bit easier than they are at home from a communication standpoint."

The Bills won two of their first three games in their new stadium and they won't be back there until November 1, so it will be a while before they get to test out any new strategies for dealing with the volume from the stands.

item.title: Kellen Moore: We will definitely have a discussion about how to start faster
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Saints followed one part of a familiar script in Monday night's loss to the Falcons when they fell behind their visitors from Atlanta early in the game.
item.content:encoded:
The Saints followed one part of a familiar script in Monday night's loss to the Falcons when they fell behind their visitors from Atlanta early in the game.

The Falcons led 14-0 in the first quarter on Monday and stretched their lead to 24-7 before halftime in New Orleans. The Saints also trailed at halftime in the first three weeks of the season, but the difference on Monday was that they weren't able to mount any kind of significant comeback in the second half.

On Tuesday, the slow starts were a topic for head coach Kellen Moore in a videoconference with reporters. The Saints have been outscored 61-26 in the first half so far this season and Moore said there is "definitely gonna be a discussion" about how to start games with a little more pep in their step.

"Logistics, scheduling, to kinda maybe adjust practice plans accordingly," Moore said. "And then, obviously, looking at what the back end looks like as far as our preparation of what we're doing early in games from a schematic standpoint. Those are really the two main areas."

One thing that would help the Saints have better control early in games would be a consistent run game that picks up yards and chews up clock. Establishing that won't be easy against a strong Vikings defense in Week 5, but Moore and company need to figure something out because consistently playing from behind isn't a recipe for piling up wins.

item.title: DeMeco Ryans: Texans blocked Cowboys' field goal by doing the same thing the Ravens did
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Texans blocked a Cowboys field goal attempt on Sunday, a week after the Ravens blocked a Cowboys field goal attempt.
item.content:encoded:
The Texans blocked a Cowboys field goal attempt on Sunday, a week after the Ravens blocked a Cowboys field goal attempt. Texans coach DeMeco Ryans says the Ravens provided the blueprint.

Ryans said on the Texans’ YouTube show that the Texans figured out how they could block a Cowboys field goal by watching film of the Ravens doing it. The Texans did the same thing and found that the Cowboys hadn't fixed their protection breakdown.

"During the film study you definitely saw a breakdown in the protection. You've seen it consistently. That's how you study film," Ryans said. "You look for those weaknesses, how you can exploit a team. We saw a weakness there in the C and D gap area."

Ryans said any time he sees film that shows the next opponent has a fundamental flaw in its protection, he's eager to see if they've fixed that flaw. The Cowboys hadn't fixed it.

"We were able to show that kick from the Baltimore game, how they were able to block it, and we're gonna design a plan similar to that to see if they fixed it. That's what all teams do. If you see a breakdown, see if they fixed it the next week," Ryans said.

It doesn't speak well for the Cowboys' coaching staff that the same flaw was there for two consecutive opponents to exploit. It's safe to say the Buccaneers will be trying to exploit the same flaw when they face the Cowboys on Thursday night.

item.title: Kyren Williams, Kenneth Walker: First players since 2016 with 2 TD runs in last 4 minutes
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: No NFL player had scored two rushing touchdowns in the final four minutes of the fourth quarter in 10 years. Then Williams and Walker did it on the same day.
item.content:encoded:
When Rams running back Kyren Williams had a touchdown run with 3:59 remaining and another touchdown run with 1:10 remaining to finish his team's fourth-quarter comeback win over the Eagles on Sunday, he was doing something that hadn't been done in the NFL in a decade: No player had scored multiple rushing touchdowns in the final four minutes of the fourth quarter of any NFL game since 2016.

Then, later on Sunday afternoon, it happened again.

With 3:21 remaining in the fourth quarter on Sunday in Las Vegas, Kansas City running back Kenneth Walker ran for a two-yard touchdown that gave the Chiefs the lead. The Raiders fumbled the ensuing kickoff, the Chiefs recovered, and on the next play Walker ran for a 22-yard touchdown that sealed the Chiefs' win.

Williams and Walker became the first NFL players in 10 years to score two rushing touchdowns in the final four minutes of the fourth quarter of an NFL game. Or, to be precise, Williams became the first player to do it in 10 years, and then Walker became the first player to do it in three hours.

Before Williams and Walker, the last player to score two rushing touchdowns in the final four minutes was Washington running back Rob Kelley, who scored had touchdown runs with 3:54 remaining and with 2:26 remaining in a win over Green Bay on November 20, 2016. Kelley was an undrafted rookie running back who surprisingly became Washington's starter midway through that season and had his greatest game that day against the Packers, carrying 24 times for 137 yards and three touchdowns. Unfortunately, Kelley never reached those heights again, and his NFL career was over two years later.

For Williams and Walker, who have been two of the NFL's top running backs for years, it's no surprise that they stepped up when their teams needed them. But their late-game heroics on Sunday represent a surprising feat for any player, let alone for two players to accomplish mere hours apart.

item.title: Rams are first NFL team to play four of their first five games in prime time
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Rams, who also will play on Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Night, epitomize the way the NFL has changed its schedule.
item.content:encoded:
When the Rams take the field against the Bills on Monday night, they'll be doing something no NFL team has ever done before: Playing their fourth prime time game within the first five games of the season.

The Rams are the first NFL team to play four of their first five games in prime time.

In Week 1, the Rams played the 49ers, in a game that kicked off on Friday morning in Australia but was televised on Thursday night in the United States. In Week 2, the Rams were on Monday Night Football against the Giants. In Week 3, the Rams were on Sunday Night Football against the Broncos. In Week 4, the Rams played their first Sunday afternoon game against the Eagles. And in Week 5, they'll be back on Monday night against the Bills.

A combination of factors led to the Rams' unusual schedule, primarily that they were expected to be the best team in the NFL, meaning the league wanted to showcase them, and the league plays a lot more prime time games than it used to. In the old days, when Monday Night Football was the only prime time slot, the NFL would never have put one team in four of the first five Monday night games. Now that there are prime time games on Sunday, Monday and Thursday every week, and occasionally other nights of the week as well, it's easier for the league to find prime time slots for marquee teams.

But when the NFL is putting the best teams in prime time, it weakens the Sunday afternoon slate. The NFL now plays more games in prime time than ever before, more Europe games on Sunday mornings than ever before, and more games on holidays than ever before, including Thanksgiving Eve, Black Friday and Christmas Day. Those games tend to feature top teams the league wants to showcase before a big audience, and those games have to come from somewhere, and that somewhere is Sunday afternoon.

After Monday night against the Bills, the Rams play their next five games on Sunday afternoon, assuming none of them are flexed into a prime time slot. But they still have a Thanksgiving Eve game against the Packers, a Thursday night game against the Chiefs and a Christmas Night game against the Seahawks ahead.

The Rams have the kind of schedule that couldn't have existed for most of NFL history.

item.title: Questions arise regarding the effectiveness of the Guardian Cap
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Guardian Cap has emerged in recent years as a new piece of football equipment.
item.content:encoded:
The Guardian Cap has emerged in recent years as a new piece of football equipment. It started as a practice device mandated by the league. More than a few players now wear it during games.

The unanswered question is whether it works. A recent item from Jeff Eisenberg of Yahoo! Sports examined the science.

"The jury is out on whether the Guardian Cap is helping NFL players," Chris Nowinski, co-founder of Boston University's CTE Center, told Eisenberg. "We have no reason to believe it's helping high school and college players.

"We've created a sort of nightmare scenario where people strap these things on their kids' helmets and believe they're now safe from concussions and CTE. Nothing could be further from the truth."

Nowinski is quoted several times in Eisenberg's article. Also quoted is NFL executive V.P. Jeff Miller, who runs both health and safety and P.R. for the league.

"I see the Guardian Cap as a transitional piece of equipment," Miller told Eisenberg. "Meaning that if the technology in the helmets continues to improve at the pace that it is right now, that will push players to the better-performing helmets, as opposed to the Guardian Cap."

The league presumably would like to see the Guardian Cap transition out of in-game use. It's bulky. It's clunky. It's a beanbag chair with an ill-fitting slipcover. In a game that derives much of its appeal from how it looks on TV, the Guardian Cap undermines the aesthetics.

And if it isn't effective, why wear it?

As one coach told PFT when the Guardian Cap first debuted in practice settings, it can lead to bad habits and create a false sense of security. Moreover, having a helmet on the helmet won't stop the brain from colliding against the inside of the skull.

Nowinski appeared on the latest episode of Pablo Torre Finds out, where he said the Guardian Cap "appears to be a bit of a scam."

“It’s very clear from their behavior and the conversations I’ve had with them," Nowinski said, "they love that the public sees the Guardian Caps, because it’s basically virtue signaling.”

Some players have opted to use the Guardian Cap in order to avoid another concussion. Two prominent examples are Saints receiver Chris Olave and Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward. Steelers rookie receiver Germie Bernard wears one specifically to protect against potential long-term cognitive issues.

"For me to play, like longevity, it’s not normal for our brains to be rattled for 10-plus years," Bernard said in August. "So that is something that can help me in the long run. That’s how I look at it.”

But their brains will still be rattled. Because, like the little ball inside a rattle, the brain is inside the skull.

With or without the Guardian Cap, modern players know the risks — and they accept them. A recent item from Kevin Seifert and Stephen Holder of ESPN included quotes from various players regarding their willingness to play pro football in exchange for what it gives them.

It's still not clear that all of them know the full extent of the risks. Chris Johnson was "shocked" to learn about the connection between football and ALS, after his diagnosis.

As Peter King explained on a special edition of #PFTPM to discuss his new book, The Game, fans, media, and players have to find a way to come to terms with still loving football despite knowing its risks. The game will always be there, replete with young men who have no qualms about putting on a helmet and rushing into the fray.

But there will also always be the Chris Johnsons, the Steve Gleasons, and the other men who develop serious neurological issues prematurely, or who spend their golden years struggling with dementia or other related conditions.

It could change once CTE can be detected in a living patient. Even then, however, the supply of twentysomethings who will happily assume the risks will continue to outweigh the demand.

item.title: Case Keenum officially listed as starting QB vs. Jets despite playing one snap
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Bears coach Ben Johnson trolled the media on Sunday, starting both Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent.
item.content:encoded:
Bears coach Ben Johnson trolled the media on Sunday, starting both Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent. Keenum took the first snap, with Bagent lined up at wide receiver.

It was the only snap for Keenum. Bagent played all 93.

An NFL spokesman said the Elias Sports Bureau clarified to the league that Keenum will be credited with the start and the victory since he is the quarterback who took the first snap.

“Good for him," Johnson said after the 23-12 win when told the win would go on Keenum's record. "I think the team gets credited for a win.”

If two quarterbacks are on the field for the first play, the one who takes the snap is considered the starter. If a running back were to take the first snap in the wildcat, with the quarterback lined up out wide, the quarterback — as the only quarterback on the field — would still get the start and the win.

Keenum is 32-36 in his career, including 2-0 as the Bears' starter this season. Bagent is 2-2.

Bagent is expected to start Sunday's game against the Packers.
